items.html: Bulgarian licence plates have the typical European design, with the blue strip on the left.

Bulgaria mainly uses the Cyrillic alphabet. However, a lot of signs will also have the Latin alphabet.

The letter “Ъ” is only found in Bulgarian and Russian, although it is fairly uncommon in Russian.

The Bulgarian word for street is улица (ulitsa), sometimes abbreviated ул. (ul.).

NOTE: In older street signs seeing only Cyrillic is more common.

Russia also uses улица/ulitsa.

There are three types of Generation 4 cars that were used to cover Bulgaria:

  • A blue car, which can be found in most European countries.
  • A red car, which is also found in Latvia, Lithuania, Russia, Slovakia, and Sweden. Of these, Russia and Slovakia are easiest to confuse with Bulgaria.
  • A black car, which is found in many European countries; of which Greece and Croatia are the ones more likely to be confused with Bulgaria.

All cars can be found with or without antenna. Additionally, you can also encounter coverage where the car is completely hidden.

The majority of Generation 3 coverage in Bulgaria was taken during March and April, resulting in very distinct dead-looking “winter” coverage.

NOTE: Hungary and Czechia also have a lot of similar dead-looking Generation 3 coverage. Furthermore, while not common, Bulgaria has some summer Generation 3.

You can commonly see a small piece of grey tape at the top of the car antenna in Generation 3 coverage. The community sometimes refers to it as “flag antenna”.

Not all Gen 3 coverage has this tape.

NOTE: This can also be seen in Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, and Romania.

Most utility poles in Bulgaria are cylindrical and made of concrete.

There is also a less common concrete ‘ladder pole’ variation. You can also sometimes see simple wooden poles.
Most poles have small, alternating hook-shaped insulators.

This style of pole top, with 3 large, alternating insulators that are shaped like upward facing hooks, is a good clue for Bulgaria. This pole top is probably unique to the country.

NOTE: You can also find this pole top with the insulators facing downwards.

Bulgarian chevrons are typically red on white.

NOTE: Many other European countries have similar chevrons. Crucially, among neighbouring countries, Romania, Turkey, and North Macedonia use the same chevrons. Greece and Serbia use black and white chevrons however. See this infographic for an overview.

Bulgarian directional signs are blue, arrow-shaped, and use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabet. Importantly, even if you are far away and cannot decipher the script, you can still see that the sign has two lines of text instead of one.
Town entry signs have a simple white design and also use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabet. Like with the directional signs, the two lines of text are obvious, even when seen from far away.

Bulgarian pedestrian signs have four stripes, and the person is wearing a hat.

NOTE: No other eastern or central European pedestrian signs have four stripes.

Bollards are generally fairly rare in Bulgaria.

When you see them, they almost always have this somewhat generic design, which is relatively similar to the bollards found in Croatia and Hungary. They have a red reflector on the front, and a white one on the back. The design isn’t terribly consistent: sometimes they are thinner, and the shape of the reflector varies.
Bulgaria usually has thin roadlines. This is particularly useful to tell Bulgaria apart from Romania, where roadlines are usually much thicker.
Bulgaria generally has fairly poor-quality roads, with many small cracks and occasionally potholes.

Most houses in Bulgaria have orange tiled roofs, with distinct patches of mortar) along the corner tiles.

Famously, Bulgarian roofs often seem poorly constructed: the roof tiles and mortar tend to be uneven, especially when compared to other European countries.

Metallic trash bins with this shape are very common in Bulgaria.

NOTE: This style of bin is also common in Turkey and other balkan countries such as Serbia, Albania and North Macedonia.

The Balkan mountains cut across Bulgaria and divide the country in two distinct halves. North of them, you will find a mostly flat area that goes all the way to the border with Romania.

The Rhodope Mountains start close to Sofia and run South-East into Greece. In them you will find the highest peaks of Bulgaria.

Between both mountain ranges you will find the second biggest flat area of Bulgaria.

The westernmost part of the country usually features many small valleys surrounded by hills and small mountains.

Area codes in Bulgaria are one of the best clues to regionguess urban rounds. Conveniently, they are ordered by first digit, so just learning the first digit can yield high results with little effort.

Numbers between parentheses in the map are area codes from a neighbouring province that frequently spill into that one.

Codes next to a small dot represent area codes unique to the province capital.

The towering mountains of Pirin and Rila National Parks can be recognised by the tall pyramid-shaped peaks, and can be seen from a few different vantage points in Blagoevgrad, Kyustendil and Sofia Provinces.
Wind turbines are most common in Dobrich Province, and usually towards the coast.
Buildings with features similar to Alpine architecture, such as white walls with brown wooden details are commonly found in and around the Smoljan region in the south.
Locations with an invisible Generation 4 Street View car can be found along the North and West borders of Bulgaria, as well as the northern half of the coast.

A red Generation 4 Street View car is mostly found in central and southeastern Bulgaria.

This car can be found with and without an antenna.

Generation 3 coverage with a piece of tape on a short antenna can be commonly found in the eastern part of Bulgaria.

NOTE: Tape antennas can very rarely appear in other provinces, the only provinces where it’s never found are Vratsa, Montana, Pazardzhik and Smolyan.

Generation 3 locations with a taped long antenna and visible white car can be found in Stara Zagora, and rarely a few small roads in Plovdiv and Burgas.

NOTE: This combination of car and antenna can be found more commonly in other European countries as well. Make sure to use other clues.

This antenna with unpeeled tape at the top, resulting in a bulkier antenna tip, can be found in the Varna Province. Coverage with this antenna is exclusively in March, resulting in a dead winter look.
The mountains overlooking Vratsa from the southwest have a very distinct “bumpy” shape, and can be seen from afar in the province.

The old town of Nessebar, and to a lesser extent Sozopol, can be recognised by the well-preserved old buildings made of a combination of unpainted stone, white stone walls and brown wood. Most of the streets are paved with cobblestone.

White street signs with two red strips; one covering the bottom and one covering part of the top, can be found in Sofia.

NOTE: You can also find other types of street signs in Sofia.
Brown street signs with bright yellow text can be found in Stara Zagora.

lm.name: Architecture - BRICK CORNICES
lm.note: Houses with prominent brick cornices below the eaves are fairly common in eastern Bulgaria, in a band from eastern Haskovo Province to Varna Province.

lm.name: Architecture - CHIMNEYS WITH MANY WINDOWS
lm.note: Chimneys with multiple openings can sometimes be found in southwestern Bulgaria, especially near Smolyan. For this clue to be reliable, the chimney must have more than three openings on a single side.

lm.name: Architecture - CINDER BLOCK WALLS, DECORATIVE PATTERNS
lm.note:
Cinder block boundary walls with repeating decorative blocks are found in eastern Bulgaria.

Note that plain cinder block walls can be found throughout the whole country.

lm.name: Architecture - CINDER BLOCK WALLS, DIAMOND PATTERN
lm.note: Cinder block walls featuring this diamond pattern are quite common in Varna Province, but do occasionally appear further north.

lm.name: Architecture - CINDER BLOCK WALLS, FLORAL PATTERN
lm.note: Cinder block walls with this four-petaled floral pattern are common in northern Burgas Province.

lm.name: Architecture - CIRCULAR CHIMNEY OPENINGS
lm.note: Circular chimney openings appear predominantly in and around Pleven Province.

lm.name: Architecture - CONCRETE WALLS WITH OVERLAPPING CIRCLE PATTERN
lm.note: Concrete boundary walls with various overlapping circle motifs are quite common across Ruse and Veliko Tarnovo provinces, but also appear occasionally across the Upper Thracian Plain.

lm.name: Architecture - CORN CRIBS
lm.note: Corn cribs are narrow, elevated, ventilated granaries for storing and drying corn, and are found mostly near the Romanian border, especially in Vratsa and Pleven provinces. They may be constructed of metal or wood.

lm.name: Architecture - IRREGULAR FLAT STONE CONSTRUCTION
lm.note: Irregularly shaped flat stone architecture can be found in several pockets across Bulgaria, as indicated on the map.The colours of the stone can range from a sandy yellow to grey. Low boundary walls made from similar stones are also common.

lm.name: Architecture - IRREGULAR RED STONE CONSTRUCTION
lm.note: Irregular dark red to purplish stone walls are characteristic of western Bulgaria. This material typically features in the foundations of buildings or in mortared boundary walls.

lm.name: Architecture - LADDER POLES
lm.note: Ladder poles can be found in virtually every part of Bulgaria, but they are significantly more common in the north and west of the country.

lm.name: Architecture - MOESIA BEIGE BRICKS
lm.note: A beige colour scheme can be seen in the architecture of some towns in the Ruse–Shumen–Veliko Tarnovo triangle. Beige brick walls are a particularly good indicator for this region. Mud bricks, light-coloured stone and beige painted walls are also common, but should only be taken as clues for this area when the entire neighbourhood is predominantly beige in colour.

lm.name: Architecture - OPEN BARNS
lm.note: Wooden barns with an open upper storey are mainly found in Vidin Province.

lm.name: Architecture - OTHER THICK CORNICES
lm.note: These thick cornices are commonly found between Plovdiv and Dobrich provinces and are also present in far northwestern Bulgaria. They can rarely be found elsewhere.

lm.name: Architecture - PENTAGONAL CHIMNEY TOPS
lm.note:
These pentagonal chimney tops, resembling a simple outline of a house, are found in the southern areas shown on the map, being most common around Plovdiv.

A similar style of chimney, where the diagonal sides have a slight overhang, can be found in parts of northern Bulgaria, most commonly in Vratsa, Pleven and Silistra provinces.

lm.name: Architecture - RECTANGLE WALL MOTIF
lm.note: Along the Romanian border in Silistra Province, you will sometimes see this repeating motif of rectangles with cut-out corners just below the eaves of buildings, with no wooden eave supports present. The colour scheme can vary.

lm.name: Architecture - RHODOPES BARNS
lm.note:
Barns in the Western Rhodopes often have a stone ground storey and a wooden upper storey. The barns sometimes have quite a towering appearance and often feature vertically arranged boards of uneven length.

Barns with a concrete ground storey can also be found in the Rhodopes, but these are a less reliable indicator for the region.

lm.name: Architecture - ROCKS ON ROOFS
lm.note: The use of loose natural stones as simple weights on top of roofs is particularly common in rural communities in the eastern half of the Balkan Mountains and in the other locations shown on the map. Elsewhere in the country, you are more likely to see bricks, pavers etc. being used in this manner instead.

lm.name: Architecture - SIMPLE BRUSH FENCES
lm.note: Boundary fences made from loose brushwood, sometimes layered on top of stone walls, are found in and near Kardzhali Province. Similar material can also be arranged into loose wattle fences in this area.

lm.name: Architecture - SIMPLE SLOPED TILE CHIMNEY
lm.note: This simple style of chimney top made from tile pieces leaning against one another to form a triangle is most common around Plovdiv and in eastern Bulgaria, and can also be found in far northwestern Bulgaria.

lm.name: Architecture - SLANTED TRIANGLE CHIMNEYS
lm.note: Chimneys with this design, formed of slanted triangular openings, are found in northeastern Bulgaria. They are most common in Razgrad, Shumen and Silistra provinces. A few can also be found near Momchilgrad in Kardzhali Province.

lm.name: Architecture - SLAT BARNS
lm.note:
Barns with walls made from horizontal wooden slats with noticeable gaps in between them are found in inland northern Bulgaria.

Barns with slats arranged diagonally, rather than horizontally, are most commonly found in Vidin Province, although they can be rarely found elsewhere in the area shown.

lm.name: Architecture - SLATE ROOF STONE VILLAGES
lm.note: If you are in a village with numerous slate-roofed houses with stone walls, you should be in one of the three distinct areas shown on the map.

lm.name: Architecture - SLATE ROOFS
lm.note: Slate roofs can be found in parts of southern Bulgaria and around the Balkan Mountains.

lm.name: Architecture - SLATE TOPPED STONE WALLS
lm.note:
Stone boundary walls topped with a single layer of slate slabs can be found in the Gabrovo–Lovech–Veliko Tarnovo triangle.

In Pavlikeni Municipality, these slate slabs are sometimes thicker and laid diagonally on top of walls rather than horizontally.

lm.name: Architecture - SOUTHWESTERN WATER TANKS
lm.note:
Long, narrow, metal water tanks can be seen on many rooftops throughout southwestern Bulgaria and also around Burgas.

While far less common, water tanks in other styles (e.g. these white tanks with coloured ends) are not reliable regional indicators.

lm.name: Architecture - STAGGERED BRICK WALLS
lm.note: Brick boundary walls with a repeating pattern of gaps are mostly found in the northern and central parts of Bulgaria shown on the map, though they can also appear south of the Balkan Mountains.

lm.name: Architecture - STAGGERED BRICK WALLS, DIAMOND PATTERN
lm.note: In Veliko Tarnovo Province, brick walls with gaps almost always use this diamond pattern.

lm.name: Architecture - STONE WALLS WITH HORIZONTAL TIMBERS
lm.note: Stone architecture featuring exposed timbers appears frequently across southern Bulgaria and less often around the Balkan Mountains. Unlike the timber-framed architecture above, these stone buildings typically feature horizontal timbers only.

lm.name: Architecture - THICK MORTAR STONE WALLS
lm.note: Architecture featuring irregular stones and thick mortar, often smeared over the stones, is indicative of southern Bulgaria.

lm.name: Architecture - TILED RIDGE ROOFS
lm.note: Corrugated-sheet roofs with tiled ridges can be found in southern and eastern Bulgaria.

lm.name: Architecture - TIMBER FRAMING WITH CLAY
lm.note:
Timber-framed architecture composed of a wooden lattice layered with smooth clay (‘wattle and daub’) is mainly found in the regions surrounding Sofia and also the regions continuing further east into the Balkan Mountains.

In western Pernik Province and western Sofia Province, you can see a variant of this with closely spaced horizontal timbers and narrow rows of clay infill.

lm.name: Architecture - TIMBER FRAMING WITH MUD BRICKS
lm.note: Timber framing with mud-brick infill is mainly found around the Central Balkan Mountains.

lm.name: Architecture - TIMBER FRAMING WITH RED BRICKS
lm.note: The distribution of timber-framed architecture in Bulgaria roughly corresponds with the hilly and mountainous regions of the country. Exposed red-brick infill can be found throughout this area.

lm.name: Architecture - TRIANGLE ATTACHMENT POLE SUPPORTS
lm.note:
In Western Bulgaria (the area covered by Electrohold), the lowest insulator support on some pole tops can have a long, solid triangular shape.

This triangular shape is usually made of a thin sheet of metal. However, if you find one that is considerably thicker, you are likely to be no further north than Sofia Province.

lm.name: Architecture - WIDE METAL BARS FENCE
lm.note: Household fences with wide metal fence posts are common across most of Silistra and Dobrich provinces.

lm.name: Architecture - WOODEN EAVE SUPPORTS
lm.note: Rows of vertical wooden supports can be found under the eaves of some buildings throughout northern and western Bulgaria.

lm.name: Architecture - WOODEN HOUSES
lm.note: Traditional wooden houses can be found in many parts of Bulgaria, but are particularly common in certain areas, most notably the Strandzha region in southern Burgas Province.

lm.name: Culture - MOSQUES
lm.note: Mosques, indicative of areas with Muslim populations, are mostly seen in northeastern Bulgaria and around the Rhodopes. There is also a significant Muslim community near Kazanlak in northern Stara Zagora Province.

lm.name: Infrastructure - “ERYUG” POLE MARKERS
lm.note: Pole markers featuring the black-and-red ‘ЕР ЮГ’ logo are found in all provinces in the EVN distribution area (southeastern Bulgaria). These are the only pole markers in Bulgaria that are physically affixed to the pole rather than painted on it.

lm.name: Infrastructure - “GOD REMONT” POLE MARKERS
lm.note: Pole markers with год ремонт (‘god. remont’ meaning ‘maintenance year’) written on them can be found in Vidin, Vratsa and Montana provinces.

lm.name: Infrastructure - “GODINA” POLE MARKERS
lm.note:
Pole markers with a row beginning with the Cyrillic letter г, which stands for година (‘godina’ meaning ‘year’), can be found primarily in Pleven and Lovech provinces.

About half the time with these pole markers, the heading for each row is followed by a printed underscore (e.g. “г ___”) which may or may not contain text. This can help to confirm your regionguess in cases where the ‘г’ is faded or otherwise illegible.

lm.name: Infrastructure - “IZVOD” POLE MARKERS
lm.note: Pole markers in the EVN distribution area (southeastern Bulgaria) usually include a row starting with извод (‘izvod’) or its abbreviations изв or из. Similar pole markings also appear in Vidin Province and the city of Kyustendil.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 7-SIDED SIGNBACK
lm.note: This seven-sided white signback sticker (which can point either up or down) is mostly found in the area shown on the map. In particular, it is virtually absent from western Bulgaria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - BLACK LOGO SIGNBACK
lm.note: This white or yellow rectangular signback sticker featuring a small black logo is mainly found in western Bulgaria. It also features two rows of bold text, placed either underneath or to the right of the logo.

lm.name: Infrastructure - BLACK MATERIAL
lm.note: Electricity wires wrapped in thick black sleeves near the insulator are particularly common in eastern Bulgaria, especially in and around Yambol Province.

lm.name: Infrastructure - BLAGOEVGRAD BLUE BULGE BUS SHELTER
lm.note: In northern Blagoevgrad Province, around Blagoevgrad and Razlog, you can find these unique blue bus shelters with walls that bulge outwards and two or three curved roof sections.

lm.name: Infrastructure - BOX POLETOP
lm.note: This pole top with a boxy shape can be found in Targovishte, Shumen and Silistra provinces.

lm.name: Infrastructure - BURGAS BOLLARDS
lm.note: The city of Burgas uses grey street bollards with a single thick red stripe.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: The city of Plovdiv uses the two styles of street sign shown in the graphic.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: Sofia City Province uses street signs with a coloured bar at the bottom and a partial bar in the same colour on the top. Various colours are used. (Note that the spa town of Devin in Smolyan Province also uses red Sofia-style signs).

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: The town of Samokov uses somewhat similar street signs to those found in Botevgrad municipality, with a darker green and different coat of arms.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: Razlog Municipality has street signs with two-tone brown bars, similar to Sofia’s colour-bar signs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: Bansko Municipality has brown street signs with the Bansko coat of arms.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: Botevgrad Municipality uses this green and white street sign.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: The city of Blagoevgrad has a yellow horse emblem on its street signs and has an unusual arrow shape.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: The town of Svilengrad uses street signs with a white top, blue bottom and a small crest.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: Sozopol Municipality uses street signs with a blue top, white bottom and a black arrow.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: The city of Stara Zagora mainly uses brown street signs with gold text and borders; however, you can sometimes find green signs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: The city of Dobrich sometimes uses some street signs with a yellow arrow design.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CITY SPECIFIC STREET SIGNS
lm.note: The city of Kardzhali uses this simple yet distinctive street sign which is white with a thin blue strip at the bottom.

lm.name: Infrastructure - CYLINDRICAL BUS SHELTERS
lm.note: Bus stop shelters with an open cylindrical shape, a bit like a tin can that has been cut in two, are most common in Pleven Province. Some also appear in Lovech and Veliko Tarnovo provinces. They can be painted in a wide range of colours.

lm.name: Infrastructure - DOBRICH POLETOP
lm.note: If you see a ‘flipped’ version of the Varna pole top, with each diagonal support above the horizontal arm instead of below it, you are most likely to be in Dobrich Province.

lm.name: Infrastructure - DOUBLE FRAME POLE MARKERS
lm.note: Pole markers with a black border formed of two rectangles can be found across northern Bulgaria, particularly in Silistra, Shumen and Varna provinces.

lm.name: Infrastructure - ELECTROHOLD & CEZ INFRASTRUCTURE
lm.note:
ЕРМ Запад (‘ERM Zapad’) is the electricity distributor for western Bulgaria, having rebranded from ЧЕЗ (CEZ) in 2022.

ЕРМ Запад has an orange logo, but it is still quite rare to find this on infrastructure visible in street view.

However, two styles of long stickers with blue text dating from before the name change can still be seen on some electricity boxes:

  • Stickers with a blue ‘E’ logo and the text ‘софия област’(Sofia Oblast) can be found in Sofia Province and the provinces south of it in the distribution area.
  • Stickers without the blue ‘E’ logo and the text ‘плевен’ (Pleven) can be found in the provinces north of Sofia Province in the distribution area.

lm.name: Infrastructure - ENERGO-PRO INFRASTRUCTURE
lm.note: ЕРП Север (‘ERP Sever’) is the electricity distributor for northeastern Bulgaria. Their blue-on-white logo is fairly common on electricity boxes in this area.

lm.name: Infrastructure - EVN & ERYUG INFRASTRUCTURE
lm.note:
ЕР ЮГ (‘ER Yug’), a subsidiary of EVN, is the electricity distributor for southeastern Bulgaria.

The black EVN logo is more common on electricity boxes. However, you can also see the red-and-black ЕР ЮГ logo on newer pole markers – see the meta in the pole marker section.

lm.name: Infrastructure - FAKE DOBRICH-VARNA POLETOP
lm.note:
This rare pole top is occasionally found in Stara Zagora and Haskovo provinces. It has a bend in the diagonal support where it reaches the pole, which can be seen if you are lucky enough to get a close-up view.

It is worth knowing mainly because it can easily be confused with the Varna and Dobrich pole tops.

lm.name: Infrastructure - GROUNDING ICON POLE MARKERS
lm.note:
Pole markers with this grounding icon (a black icon resembling an inverted Christmas tree) are found in much of the Electrohold energy distribution area (western Bulgaria).

Note that you can also see pole markers with this icon in the Svilengrad area of Haskovo Province. These always feature either the text извод (‘izvod’) or one of its abbreviations, ‘изв’ or ‘из’.

lm.name: Infrastructure - HANGING INSULATORS
lm.note: Hanging insulators are mainly found in northeastern Bulgaria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - HUNGARY-STYLE HIGHWAY BOLLARDS
lm.note: Highway bollards similar to those found in Hungary are used throughout the country, but they are relatively uncommon outside northeastern Bulgaria. They can be solid and wedge-shaped or thin and curved.

lm.name: Infrastructure - IZVOD LETTERS
lm.note: ‘Izvod’ pole markers that are labelled alphabetically (e.g. ‘изв B’) are found in the regions shown, notably including Pleven and Stara Zagora provinces, as well as in southern Kardzhali Province.

lm.name: Infrastructure - IZVOD MARKERS WITH TALL FRAMES
lm.note: ‘Izvod’ pole markers with tall black frames (i.e. taller than they are wide) are typically seen in Haskovo and Kardzhali provinces.

lm.name: Infrastructure - IZVOD MARKERS WITH WIDE FRAMES
lm.note: ‘Izvod’ pole markers with wide black frames are found towards the east, mainly Sliven and Burgas provinces.

lm.name: Infrastructure - IZVOD NUMBERS
lm.note: ‘Izvod’ pole markers that are labelled numerically (e.g. ‘изв 4’) instead of alphabetically are found in these areas, which include all the provinces bordering Turkey.

lm.name: Infrastructure - IZVOD WITH “№”
lm.note: ‘Izvod’ pole markers with a row labelled “№” (without “ст”) are found most often in Yambol Province, but can be seen as far west as Pazardzhik.

lm.name: Infrastructure - IZVOD WITH “ST”
lm.note: ‘Izvod’ pole markers with a row labelled “ст” (without the №) appear in four clear clusters: Burgas and Sliven provinces, Haskovo Province, northern Pazardzhik Province, and Vidin Province.

lm.name: Infrastructure - IZVOD WITH “STALB №”
lm.note:
‘Izvod’ pole markers featuring a row labelled ‘ст №’ (meaning ‘pole number’) are found in the western part of the EVN distribution area.

Note that nearly all ‘ст №’ pole markers without an ‘izvod’ line instead have a ‘год ремонт’ line. Based on that meta, these should be found in northwestern Bulgaria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - KARDZHALI BUS SHELTERS
lm.note: In the south of Kardzhali Province, including Momchilgrad, Krumovgrad and Kirkovo municipalities, you can find these green or blue bus shelters with a yellow strip across the front. The yellow strip sometimes includes the municipality (община) or town name.

lm.name: Infrastructure - LEFT SIDE WARNING SIGNBACK
lm.note:
Signback stickers featuring a red, downward-pointing triangle ‘warning’ symbol on the left side of the sticker are mostly found in Varna Province, and more generally in northeastern Bulgaria.

Note that stickers with a centred, upward-pointing ‘warning’ symbol can be found across the whole country, but are virtually absent from the northeast of the country.

lm.name: Infrastructure - MARITSA COMPLEX
lm.note:
The Maritsa Power Plant complex has three main plants in the southeast of Stara Zagora Province. Each plant features large cooling towers or smoke stacks that can be recognised from far away in the vast, flat landscape of the Upper Thracian Plain.

Other comparably large power plants in Bulgaria are located in hillier or more urban settings.

lm.name: Infrastructure - NORTHEASTERN POLETOP
lm.note: In northeastern Bulgaria, you can find similar pole tops, but the support reaches the end of the horizontal arm, forming a narrower triangular opening.

lm.name: Infrastructure - ORANGE CIRCLE SIGNBACK
lm.note: Signback stickers with an orange circular shape also tend to appear in eastern Bulgaria, but their distribution is more widespread.

lm.name: Infrastructure - PERNIK POLE MARKERS
lm.note:
In Pernik Province, pole markers usually have minimal text, often just a single letter above a number that is one or two digits.

These markings often have a ‘tombstone’ shape, allowing them to be recognised at a distance even without the black text. Sometimes an empty ‘tombstone’ marking can accompany a rectangular marking with the text. However, a similar shape rarely appears in other provinces, so use this tip with caution.

lm.name: Infrastructure - PERNIK/SOFIA POLE MARKERS
lm.note: Similar pole markings, with a letter above two rows of numbers, the top row having one digit and the lower row (indicating the year) having two digits, can be found in Pernik and Sofia provinces. This format is slightly more typical in the western parts of both provinces.

lm.name: Infrastructure - PLOVDIV BOLLARDS
lm.note: The city of Plovdiv uses these street bollards with exactly three black stripes and two yellow stripes.

lm.name: Infrastructure - RECTANGLE AND CIRCLE SIGNBACK
lm.note: This signback sticker has a distinctive shape with a circle overlapping the top-right corner of a rectangle. It can be found nationwide, but is much more common in southern Bulgaria, as well as in the Shumen and Targovishte area.

lm.name: Infrastructure - RECTANGULAR POLETOP
lm.note: This pole top has supports which form openings shaped like a rectangle with an elongated corner. It is most common in Ruse, Razgrad and Silistra provinces, but appears occasionally elsewhere.

lm.name: Infrastructure - RED OCTAGON SIGNBACK
lm.note:
This red octagonal sticker (resembling a stop sign) is mainly found in Shumen and Varna provinces, as well as in northern Burgas Province.

Note that from a distance, these stickers can be confused with the orange circular signback stickers mentioned below.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SKINNY HOLEY POLES
lm.note: Holey poles are sometimes found in northern Bulgaria, especially around the city of Veliko Tarnovo.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SOFIA CITY PROVINCE BUS STOP TRASH BIN
lm.note: Bus stops in Sofia City Province can have a wide variety of sign and shelter styles. However, one piece of infrastructure is remarkably consistent: these dark grey rubbish bins with two yellow stripes. You can find one at virtually every bus stop in the region, including at most bus stops without shelters.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SOFIA HOLEY POLES
lm.note:
More rarely, you will also find a variant of these holey poles in and around Sofia Province. These can be distinguished from regular holey poles by the indent on the bars in between the holes.

Additionally, very wide holey poles, which are always this variant, are only found in this region.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SOFIA PROVINCE POLE MARKERS
lm.note: In Sofia Province, you can see pole markers with two rows of text spaced far apart. The format of the text itself varies, and the text can be positioned in the corners of the pole marker. Sometimes there is a red lightning bolt icon between the two rows, but often it is absent.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SOFIA THICK BOLLARDS
lm.note:
These thick ‘street bollards’ with two stripes can be found in the city of Sofia. There are two characteristic colour schemes: black with yellow, orange or white stripes, and yellow with white stripes.

The yellow-on-black design is easy to remember, as it matches the Sofia City Province bus stop bin.

Note that the white-on-yellow style also appears rarely in the city of Burgas.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SOFIA WHITE NUMBERS
lm.note: In Sofia City Province, you can see vertical white numbers written on some poles.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SOUTHEASTERN POLETOP
lm.note:
In southeastern Bulgaria, you often find pole tops with supports reaching about halfway across the horizontal arm, forming a wide triangular opening.

This is the only pole top in southeastern Bulgaria that ever has hanging insulators.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SPELLED OUT “IZVOD” MARKERS
lm.note: ‘Izvod’ pole markers that use the full word извод instead of an abbreviation are generally found in Burgas, Sliven and Stara Zagora provinces.

lm.name: Infrastructure - SQUARE “EARS” BUS SHELTER
lm.note: Bus shelters with two protruding square shapes on either side of the roof, almost resembling ears, can be found in the centre-north of Bulgaria as shown on the map. The colour schemes of these shelters vary.

lm.name: Infrastructure - STARA ZAGORA BOLLARDS
lm.note: The city of Stara Zagora uses grey street bollards with a single orange stripe. This bollard may rarely appear outside the city in Stara Zagora Province.

lm.name: Infrastructure - THIN INSULATORS
lm.note: Insulators that are unusually thin are mostly used in eastern Bulgaria, and especially in the southeast of the country.

lm.name: Infrastructure - TRAM TRACKS
lm.note: Sofia is the only city in Bulgaria with tram tracks embedded in the roads. In other Bulgarian cities, you can find trolleybus systems with overhead wires, but no tracks.

lm.name: Infrastructure - VARNA POLETOP
lm.note: This variant of the northeastern pole top above occurs mostly in Varna Province and neighbouring parts of Shumen and Dobrich provinces. It has two diagonal supports for each insulator (one on either side of the pole). Each of these crosses the pole, rather than stopping when it reaches the pole.

lm.name: Infrastructure - WIND TURBINES
lm.note: Wind turbines are most common in southern Dobrich Province, but can be found in several other regions of the country as well.

lm.name: Landscape - BELOGRADCHIK ROCK FORMATIONS
lm.note: In the town of Belogradchik and some surrounding areas, you might spot these unique towering, pillared rock formations.

lm.name: Landscape - BLAGOEVGRAD SANDY CLIFFS
lm.note: Steep sandstone escarpments, such as the Melnik Earth Pyramids, can be seen in southern Blagoevgrad Province.

lm.name: Landscape - CHUPRENE MOUNTAINS
lm.note: Chuprene Municipality in Vidin Province is very mountainous, containing the highest peak in the Western Balkan Mountains. Mountains here often have a distinctive asymmetrical ‘wave-like’ appearance.

lm.name: Landscape - EASTERN RHODOPES
lm.note:
The Rhodope Mountains (often simply ‘the Rhodopes’) are a mountain range spanning most of the border between Bulgaria and Greece.

The Eastern Rhodopes, which run through Kardzhali and Haskovo provinces, are typically much drier and more open than the Western Rhodopes and have less coniferous forest. It is common to see scattered rocks and stone walls in the Eastern Rhodopes.

The Eastern Rhodopes are also more hilly than mountainous, which can help distinguish them from the Western Rhodopes, although some taller mountains can still be found.

lm.name: Landscape - FLAT SANDY HILLS
lm.note: Unusually flat-topped hills can be seen between the cities of Shumen and Varna, and to the south of Shumen. These hills often have exposed limestone slopes but can also be covered in trees. You may also occasionally spot rocky escarpments.

lm.name: Landscape - MOESIA ROCK VALLEYS
lm.note: In the Ruse–Shumen–Veliko Tarnovo triangle, you can sometimes find fairly low, rugged limestone cliff faces. This whole area is slightly hilly, in contrast to other parts of the Danubian Plain.

lm.name: Landscape - PIRIN & RILA
lm.note: Pirin and Rila National Parks both feature dramatic, towering mountains which can have pyramid-like peaks. These are the only mountains in Bulgaria that commonly feature snowcaps in summer.

lm.name: Landscape - ROSE VALLEY
lm.note: The Rose Valley is the relatively narrow valley just south of the Central Balkan Mountains. It is quite flat and heavily cultivated, and is often easy to recognise because of the E-W mountain ranges that you can frequently see quite nearby to both the north and south.

lm.name: Landscape - SHUMEN MONUMENT
lm.note: The Monument to 1300 Years of Bulgaria can be spotted to the south from various locations in the city of Shumen.

lm.name: Landscape - SLIVENSKA PLANINA
lm.note: Slivenska Planina is a section of the Eastern Balkan Mountains that forms a craggy grey wall immediately to the north of the city of Sliven, making it easy to identify the city. Another useful landmark for identifying Sliven is the large white cross on a forested peak slightly to the west of the Slivenska Planina ridge.

lm.name: Landscape - STEEP GRAY CLIFF LANDSCAPES
lm.note: Tall mountain rock faces, usually of grey rock, are generally found in two areas: the western half of the Balkan Mountains, and the southern Rila–Rhodope Massif.

lm.name: Landscape - STRUMA VALLEY
lm.note: The warm, southern portion of the Struma River Valley is notable for its Mediterranean climate and features many large vineyards as well as areas with greenhouses. It is flanked by N-S mountain ridges on either side.

lm.name: Landscape - TREE-LINED FIELDS
lm.note: Most of Dobrich Province has an extremely distinctive landscape, featuring flat farm fields that are often divided by long rows of trees running perpendicular to the road.

lm.name: Landscape - VITOSHA
lm.note: Vitosha is a gradually sloping but very prominent mountain south of Sofia, serving as a useful reference point for identifying the flatter valley surrounding the city.

lm.name: Landscape - YAMBOL FREEDOM MONUMENT
lm.note: The Monument to 110 Years of Freedom can be seen slightly to the east of the city of Yambol.

lm.name: SOFIA HOLEY POLES
lm.note: More rarely, you will also find a variant of these holey poles in and around Sofia Province. These can be distinguished from regular holey poles by the indent on the bars in between the holes.

lm.name: Vegetation - CORN
lm.note: Corn is found throughout much of Bulgaria but is most commonly seen in the north.

lm.name: Vegetation - DOG ROSE
lm.note: Dog rose (Rosa canina) is a shrub with characteristic pinkish-white, five-petaled flowers. It is mostly found in northern and western Bulgaria.

lm.name: Vegetation - FIR
lm.note: Fir trees (Abies alba) can look very similar to spruces, but, unlike spruces, their branches resemble a flat fan shape. They are found in some of the highest altitude areas of the country i.e. the Western Rhodopes, Pirin National Park and Rila National Park.

lm.name: Vegetation - FIREWEED
lm.note: Fireweed (Chamaenerion angustifolium) is found in high-altitude areas in the southwest of the country and specifically in the Western Rhodopes, Rila National Park and Vitosha National Park. It can be recognised by its pink flowers, spear-shaped inflorescence and thin leaves.

lm.name: Vegetation - LAVENDER FIELDS
lm.note: Lavender is easily recognised by its purple flowers and is usually grown in ‘clumpy’ rows, making it identifiable even when it is not in flower. It is most commonly seen in Dobrich Province and in central Bulgaria.

lm.name: Vegetation - MULLEIN
lm.note: Mullein (Verbascum spp.) has a wide range but is predominantly found in the western half of Bulgaria. It is easily recognised by its candelabra-like yellow inflorescence.

lm.name: Vegetation - OAK FORESTS
lm.note: While individual oaks (Quercus spp.) are not useful for regionguessing, forests dominated by oak are a good indicator for southeastern Bulgaria. Oak trees can be identified by the characteristic lobed shape of their leaves.

lm.name: Vegetation - RAPESEED
lm.note: Rapeseed can be recognised by its yellow flowers and is particularly common in Yambol Province.

lm.name: Vegetation - SCOTS PINE
lm.note: Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) can be recognised by its red trunk, with the bottom section of the trunk being darker and more brown rather than red. It is found in all the mountainous regions but is particularly common and abundant in the Rhodopes.

lm.name: Vegetation - SPRUCE
lm.note: Spruce trees (Picea abies) can be recognised by their drooping branches with the secondary branches hanging down from the primary branch. They are found in the southwestern mountains and, less commonly, the Central Balkan mountains.

lm.name: Vegetation - TEASEL
lm.note: Teasel (Dipsacus laciniatus) can be recognised by its spiky flower head. The tough structure of the plant is highly resilient, allowing its dried seedheads to remain standing after the plant has died. It is especially common around Sofia and Pernik. You can also find it less commonly in the other areas shown on the map.

lm.name: Vegetation - VINEYARDS
lm.note: Vineyards can be found in a few pockets throughout Bulgaria, particularly in the Upper Thracian Plain.

lm.name: Vegetation - VIPER’S BUGLOSS
lm.note: Viper’s bugloss (Echium vulgare) is recognisable by its blue-purple flowers that are each individually attached to a central stem by a small flower stalk (rather than being directly attached to the stem). It is particularly common in the Western Rhodopes.

lm.name: Bollards
lm.note:
Bollards are generally fairly rare in Bulgaria.

When you see them, they almost always have this somewhat generic design, which is relatively similar to the bollards found in Croatia and Hungary. They have a red reflector on the front, and a white one on the back. The design isn’t terribly consistent: sometimes they are thinner, and the shape of the reflector varies.

lm.name: Patches Of Mortar
lm.note:
• Most houses in Bulgaria have orange tiled roofs, with distinct patches of mortar along the corner tiles.

Famously, Bulgarian roofs often seem poorly constructed:

  • The roof tiles and mortar tend to be uneven, especially when compared to other European countries.

lm.name: Chevrons
lm.note:
• Bulgarian chevrons are typically red on white.

--- NOTE:

  • Many other European countries have similar chevrons.
  • Crucially, among neighbouring countries, Romania, Turkey, and North Macedonia use the same chevrons.
  • Greece and Serbia use black and white chevrons however.

lm.name: Ghetto-Like Look
lm.note: • Suburbs in Bulgaria are generally among the poorest areas in Europe, with small, densely built houses and generally an almost ghetto-like look.

lm.name: South - Alpine Architecture
lm.note: • Buildings with features similar to Alpine architecture, such as white walls with brown wooden details are commonly found in and around the Smoljan region in the south.

lm.name: Bulgaria
lm.note:
Conveniently, they are ordered by first digit, so just learning the first digit can yield high results with little effort.

Numbers between parentheses in the map are area codes from a neighbouring province that frequently spill into that one.

Codes next to a small dot represent area codes unique to the province capital.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner
lm.name: Alternating pole top
lm.note: This style of pole top, featuring 3 large, alternating insulators shaped like upward-facing hooks, is a good clue for Bulgaria. This pole top is likely unique to the country.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner
lm.name: Small alternating hooks
lm.note: Most poles in Bulgaria have small, alternating hook-shaped insulators, which can also be found in other countries (mostly on wooden poles, like Latvia, North Macedonia, and a few others). However, if you see them on a concrete pole, you're most likely in Bulgaria. Try using other clues to confirm.

lm.name: 4 Stripes + Hat Bulgaria
lm.note: Hat - Austria, Bulgaria, Czechia, Slovakia. > those with 4 Zebra Stripes: Bulgaria.

lm.name: Town signs
lm.note: Town entry signs in Bulgaria have a simple white design and use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets. Like directional signs, the two lines of text are clear and visible even from a distance.

lm.name: Bulgarian
lm.note:
Bulgarian is a South Slavic language, closely related to Macedonian. Bulgarian mainly uses the Cyrillic alphabet, but many signs are written in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts. The letter Ъ is only found in Bulgarian and Russian, although it is fairly uncommon in Russian, and is thus a good way to identify Bulgarian.

The Bulgarian word for street is улица (ulitsa), sometimes abbreviated ул. (ul.). This is the same as most Slavic languages (Russian, Serbian...).

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Bulgaria usually has thin roadlines.
  • This is particularly useful to tell Bulgaria apart from Romania, where roadlines are usually much thicker.

lm.name: Alternating pole top
lm.note: Most poles have small, alternating hook-shaped insulators.

lm.name: small alternating hooks
lm.note:
This style of pole top, with 3 large, alternating insulators that are shaped like upward facing hooks, is a good clue for Bulgaria. This pole top is probably unique to the country.

NOTE: You can also find this pole top with the insulators facing downwards.

lm.name: Plovdiv
lm.note: These 2 street signs can be found in Plovdiv, the left one is more common.

lm.name: Sofia
lm.note:
White street signs with two red strips; one covering the bottom and one covering part of the top, can be found in Sofia.

NOTE: You can also find other types of street signs in Sofia.

lm.name: Stara Zagora street sign
lm.note: Brown street signs with bright yellow text can be found in Stara Zagora.

lm.name: Alpine architecture
lm.note: Buildings with features similar to Alpine architecture, such as white walls with brown wooden details are commonly found in and around the Smoljan region in the south. Lots of pine trees are also commonly seen.

lm.name: Balkan Mountain trekker
lm.note: This trekker is found on the Balkan mountain. The trekker is divided in 2 parts, you can see huge green lush mountains with exposed grey rock in the northern half. The southern half is just a forest with steep elevation.

lm.name: Black dots on the road
lm.note:
The 11 and 15 that goes from Oryahovo to Vratsa has this distinct road with a tremendous amount of black dots on it (idk what its called). This kind of road is also found in the south on the 6 between Radomir and Izvor. And a small part of the 1 around Mursalevo. (mountainous = south, flat = north, beware that the 15 towards Vratsa gets huge mountains towards the south)

NOTE: There are a very few other roads elsewhere in Bulgaria that also have the dots but are more greyish and are less distinct. Make sure the road really has that distinct look with the clear black dots on them.

lm.name: Bulkier antenna tip
lm.note: This antenna with unpeeled tape at the top, resulting in a bulkier antenna tip, can be found in the Varna Province. Coverage with this antenna is exclusively in March, resulting in a dead winter look.

lm.name: Dense pine trees
lm.note: Dense pine trees are super common in the south of Bulgaria, specifically in the province of Smolyan, the southern half of Pazardzhik, East Blagoevgrad and small areas around them.

lm.name: Distinct valley
lm.note:
This long stretched region south of the Balkan Mountains can be recognized by the flat agriculture landscape, with a big mountain ridge to the north and smaller mountains/hills to the south. You can also sometimes see tiny hills/mountains to your east/west. (Tip for memorizing: From Rozino to Sliven).

The region south/south-east of Sliven has little to no hills to the south, but still has the distinct mountain ridge to the north aswell as small hills towards the east/west.

NOTE: There are a few other smaller regions with smaller mountains that can have a similar appearance, their either more towards the west or east.

lm.name: Flat landscape
lm.note:
East Dobrich is by far the flattest region of bulgaria, it will either be completely flat or you will notice very little elevation. Rows of trees are commonly seen next to the road and in the distance. Landscape itself is very agriculture and you will almost never see hills in this region (they become more common towards the west).

Also wind turbines can often be seen towards the south-east.

lm.name: Invisible Gen 4 car
lm.note: Locations with an invisible Generation 4 Street View car can be found along the North and West borders of Bulgaria, as well as the northern half of the coast.

lm.name: Long antenna with tape
lm.note:
Generation 3 locations with a taped long antenna and visible white car can be found in Stara Zagora, and rarely a few small roads in Plovdiv and Burgas.

NOTE: This combination of car and antenna can be found more commonly in other European countries as well. Make sure to use other clues.

lm.name: Musala trekker
lm.note: This trekker is found on the Musala mountain. You can often see a mountain ridge to the west, part of the trekker is on the ridge itself. Other mountains are seen on the east. Its very rocky with lots of small pine trees.

lm.name: Nessebar/Sozopol
lm.note: The old town of Nessebar, and to a lesser extent Sozopol, can be recognised by the well-preserved old buildings made of a combination of unpainted stone, white stone walls and brown wood. Most of the streets are paved with cobblestone.

lm.name: Pirin trekker
lm.note: This trekker is found on top of Pirin National Park. It has a tremendous amount of white/grey rocks laying around. With lots of small bushes.

lm.name: Plovdiv region
lm.note:
This big region surrounding Plovdiv can be recognized by the very large flat agriculture landscape, and you can almost always see big mountain ridges to the north and the south. Its possible that you can't see the mountains on one side because your too far north or south. But even then its still recognizable. Also the mountains to the south are bigger than the mountains north.

The region around Pazardzhik can also look quite similar but has random hills and is less flat.

lm.name: Plovdiv street signs
lm.note: Plovdiv has these 2 unique street signs. The one on the left is more common.

lm.name: Pyramid shaped peaks
lm.note: The towering mountains of Pirin and Rila National Parks can be recognised by the tall pyramid-shaped peaks, and can be seen from a few different vantage points in Blagoevgrad, Kyustendil and Sofia Provinces.

lm.name: Red gen 4 car
lm.note:
A red Generation 4 Street View car is mostly found in central and southeastern Bulgaria.

This car can be found with and without an antenna.

lm.name: Short antenna with tape
lm.note:
Generation 3 coverage with a piece of tape on a short antenna can be commonly found in the eastern part of Bulgaria.

NOTE: Tape antennas can very rarely appear in other provinces, the only provinces where it’s never found are Vratsa, Montana, Pazardzhik and Smolyan.

lm.name: Sliven white cross
lm.note: You can often see this big white cross on the top of a mountain to the north/east in and around Sliven. It can be a little hard to see sometimes so make sure to zoom in and identify it.

lm.name: Sofia street sign
lm.note:
White street signs with two red strips (can rarely be blue or green); one covering the bottom and one covering part of the top, can be found in Sofia.

NOTE: You can also find other types of street signs in Sofia.

lm.name: Stara Zagora street sign
lm.note: Brown street signs with bright yellow text can be found in Stara Zagora.

lm.name: Vitosha Mountain
lm.note: The Vitosha Mountain south of Sofia can be recognized by its huge and long dome-like shape. You can often see tall buildings beneath it and it can be seen from far away. A ridge of mountains can also be seen in the south and the landscape around it is pretty flat and agriculture.

lm.name: Vratsa mountains
lm.note: The mountains overlooking Vratsa from the southwest have a very distinct “bumpy” shape, and can be seen from afar in the province.

lm.name: Wind turbines
lm.note: Wind turbines are most common in Dobrich Province, and usually towards the coast.

top.html: Bulgarian licence plates have the typical European design, with the blue strip on the left.

top.html:
Bulgaria mainly uses the Cyrillic alphabet. However, a lot of signs will also have the Latin alphabet.

The letter “Ъ” is only found in Bulgarian and Russian, although it is fairly uncommon in Russian.
top.raw: Bulgaria mainly uses the **Cyrillic alphabet**. However, a lot of signs will also have the Latin alphabet. The letter “Ъ” is only found in Bulgarian and Russian, although it is fairly uncommon in Russian.

top.html:
The Bulgarian word for street is улица (ulitsa), sometimes abbreviated ул. (ul.).

NOTE: In older street signs seeing only Cyrillic is more common.

Russia also uses улица/ulitsa.
top.raw: The Bulgarian word for street is **улица** (ulitsa), sometimes abbreviated **ул.** (ul.). NOTE: In older street signs seeing only Cyrillic is more common. Russia also uses улица/ulitsa.

top.html:
There are three types of Generation 4 cars that were used to cover Bulgaria:

  • A blue car, which can be found in most European countries.
  • A red car, which is also found in Latvia, Lithuania, Russia, Slovakia, and Sweden. Of these, Russia and Slovakia are easiest to confuse with Bulgaria.
  • A black car, which is found in many European countries; of which Greece and Croatia are the ones more likely to be confused with Bulgaria.

All cars can be found with or without antenna. Additionally, you can also encounter coverage where the car is completely hidden.
top.raw: There are three types of Generation 4 cars that were used to cover Bulgaria: - A **blue** car, which can be found in most European countries. - A **red** car, which is also found in Latvia, Lithuania, Russia, Slovakia, and Sweden. Of these, Russia and Slovakia are easiest to confuse with Bulgaria. - A **black** car, which is found in many European countries; of which Greece and Croatia are the ones more likely to be confused with Bulgaria. All cars can be found with or without antenna. Additionally, you can also encounter coverage where the car is completely hidden.

top.html:
The majority of Generation 3 coverage in Bulgaria was taken during March and April, resulting in very distinct dead-looking “winter” coverage.

NOTE: Hungary and Czechia also have a lot of similar dead-looking Generation 3 coverage. Furthermore, while not common, Bulgaria has some summer Generation 3.
top.raw: The majority of Generation 3 coverage in Bulgaria was taken during March and April, resulting in very distinct dead-looking “winter” coverage. NOTE: Hungary and Czechia also have a lot of similar dead-looking Generation 3 coverage. Furthermore, while not common, Bulgaria has some [summer Generation 3](https://www.google.com/maps/@42.6462065,24.980028,3a,90y,176.39h,83.7t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1srReAyNGYfJcuvSNTXNt4tQ!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu).

top.html:
You can commonly see a small piece of grey tape at the top of the car antenna in Generation 3 coverage. The community sometimes refers to it as “flag antenna”.

Not all Gen 3 coverage has this tape.

NOTE: This can also be seen in Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, and Romania.
top.raw: You can commonly see a small piece of **grey tape **at the top of the car antenna in Generation 3 coverage. The community sometimes refers to it as “flag antenna”. Not all Gen 3 coverage has this tape. NOTE: This can also be seen in Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, and Romania.

top.html:
Most utility poles in Bulgaria are cylindrical and made of concrete.

There is also a less common concrete ‘ladder pole’ variation. You can also sometimes see simple wooden poles.
top.raw: Most utility poles in Bulgaria are **cylindrical **and made of **concrete**. There is also a less common concrete ‘ladder pole’ variation. You can also sometimes see simple wooden poles.
Most poles have small, alternating **hook-shaped** insulators.

top.html:
This style of pole top, with 3 large, alternating insulators that are shaped like upward facing hooks, is a good clue for Bulgaria. This pole top is probably unique to the country.

NOTE: You can also find this pole top with the insulators facing downwards.
top.raw: This style of pole top, with 3 large, alternating insulators that are shaped like **upward facing hooks**, is a good clue for Bulgaria. This pole top is probably unique to the country. NOTE: You can also find this pole top with the insulators facing [downwards](https://maps.app.goo.gl/srfTSgJK7kcGUUQNA).

top.html:
Bulgarian chevrons are typically red on white.

NOTE: Many other European countries have similar chevrons. Crucially, among neighbouring countries, Romania, Turkey, and North Macedonia use the same chevrons. Greece and Serbia use black and white chevrons however. See this infographic for an overview.
top.raw: Bulgarian chevrons are typically **red on white**. NOTE: Many other European countries have similar chevrons. Crucially, among neighbouring countries, Romania, Turkey, and North Macedonia use the same chevrons. Greece and Serbia use black and white chevrons however. [See this infographic](/images/bulgaria/eu_chevrons.png?) for an overview.

top.html: Bulgarian directional signs are blue, arrow-shaped, and use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabet. Importantly, even if you are far away and cannot decipher the script, you can still see that the sign has two lines of text instead of one.
top.raw: Bulgarian directional signs are blue, arrow-shaped, and use both the **Cyrillic and Latin** alphabet. Importantly, even if you are far away and cannot decipher the script, you can still see that the sign has two lines of text instead of one.

top.html: Town entry signs have a simple white design and also use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabet. Like with the directional signs, the two lines of text are obvious, even when seen from far away.
top.raw: Town entry signs have a simple white design and also use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabet. Like with the directional signs, the two lines of text are obvious, even when seen from far away.
